With the M6 Mac mini and its more powerful M5 Pro version officially going on sale, Apple has quietly removed one of the machine's most appealing selling points. Although the two new Mac minis look identical to the previous generation on the outside, Apple has taken away a hidden feature that made the previous Mac mini an incredible bargain.

When the M4 Mac mini first launched, its value-for-money was off the charts. Besides featuring Apple's own M4 SoC, it also came standard with 16GB of unified memory, three Thunderbolt 4 ports, two front-facing USB 3 ports, HDMI, and Ethernet. Priced at US$599, with a student price as low as US$499, the M4 Mac mini was not only the most versatile Mac across Apple's entire product line, but also the best in terms of overall capability.

Video: Apple Killed the Mac mini's Best Hidden Feature :(

However, this smallest Mac from Apple had another killer feature that made it even more valuable: a built-in upgradeable storage slot. Users could simply pry open the back panel, unscrew a few screws, and access a removable NAND module, easily swapping in third-party SSDs of up to 2TB.

This design brought multiple benefits. Users could not only upgrade their SSD or easily deal with hard drive failures, but also save quite a bit of money—no need to choose Apple's custom upgrade options, just buy a much cheaper third-party SSD and you're sorted.

At the time, Apple priced the 2TB upgrade at US$800, so simply ticking that option would turn this "budget" computer into a US$1,400 machine. By purchasing the machine and upgrading with a third-party SSD afterwards, users could save nearly US$500.

As someone who enjoys building PCs myself, I was naturally thrilled, and I even made a complete video tutorial demonstrating step by step how to upgrade the original SSD with a third-party drive. The video received a pretty enthusiastic response, accumulating 500,000 views.

Video: How to Upgrade the M4 Mac mini SSD

Good times don't last.

After this generation of Mac mini launched, Apple soldered the SSD directly onto the motherboard, completely eliminating the possibility for users to upgrade with third-party NAND modules after purchase.

The Mac mini has gone from being the undisputed best-value Mac to a product that is significantly more expensive—not only has the base model jumped from US$600 to US$900, but the 2TB upgrade has also gone from US$800 to US$1,000.

At current prices, if you want an M6 Mac mini with 2TB SSD, you'll inevitably be handing Apple US$1,900. For the previous M4 Mac mini, including the then US$320 post-purchase upgrade price, getting to 2TB capacity cost roughly US$920. Of course, prices fluctuate over time and cannot be compared directly in a straightforward way (compared with Apple, you know what I mean), but the price here is a full US$1,000 more. Beyond Apple raising prices aggressively, the bigger reason is that they have directly stripped users of the right to upgrade themselves.

Regarding Apple making the base Mac mini US$300 more expensive, I can roughly guess the reason, and the surge in SSD prices is something I can understand as well. Driven by factors like AI, the costs of components, SSDs, and memory have all risen significantly. But none of this explains why Apple chose to solder the SSD to the motherboard instead of retaining the previous user-replaceable design.

Why did Apple decide to go back to the old approach of soldering the SSD? We can speculate, but we'll never know the real answer. What is certain is that the prices of these machines have risen substantially—saying "substantially" might even be an understatement. Comparing the M4 Mac mini with a 2TB post-purchase upgrade back then to the M6 Mac mini with a 2TB custom upgrade now, the price has gone up by approximately 106%.

9to5Mac Opinion

Finding a base model M4 Mac mini at a reasonable price on the second-hand market these days isn't exactly easy, but if you do manage to find one, it remains an excellent machine in terms of performance, features, and upgradeable SSD.

The only good news is that all Mac mini models come with Thunderbolt connectivity, allowing users to easily add high-speed external storage via USB or Thunderbolt SSDs. Personally, I'm particularly fond of the Samsung T9, which is a relatively affordable storage expansion solution.

Why do you think Apple abandoned the user-replaceable SSD design on the Mac mini? Do you have any unique insights? Feel free to share your thoughts in the comments section.
